title: Random Oracle Model — Heuristic vs Reality

questions.question: What is the key property of a random oracle that distinguishes it from a concrete hash function?
options: Its outputs are truly uniformly random for each new input and can be programmed by the simulator
It is faster to compute than SHA-256
It has a fixed input length
It is collision-free by construction
questions.explanation: A random oracle is lazy-sampled (truly random per new input) and programmable. Concrete hash functions are deterministic and efficiently computable without querying an oracle — they cannot be programmed by a simulator.

questions.question: A 256-bit hash function provides how many bits of collision security (birthday bound)?
options: 128 bits — a birthday attack needs 2^128 queries
256 bits — collisions are as hard as preimages
64 bits — birthday attacks always halve the security
192 bits — the birthday bound loses one third of bits
questions.explanation: Birthday bound: collision probability ≈ 1/2 after q ≈ 2^(n/2) queries. For n=256: q ≈ 2^128. So collision security = 128 bits, not 256.

questions.question: An adversary makes q=2^40 queries to a 256-bit random oracle. What is the preimage-finding advantage?
options: 1 — 40 bits of queries always find a preimage
2^{-40} — the advantage equals 1/q
questions.explanation: Preimage bound: q/2^n = 2^40 / 2^256 = 2^{-216}. Each query hits the target independently with probability 2^{-256}; union bound over 2^40 queries.

questions.question: What is 'programmability' of the random oracle and why does it matter for reductions?
options: The simulator can pre-set H(x*) = v before the adversary queries x*, enabling embedding of a hard problem instance
The adversary can reprogram H after querying it to change outputs
The hash output can be truncated to any desired length
The reduction can rewind the adversary to replay queries
questions.explanation: Programmability: the simulator controls the RO and sets H(x*) = challenge before the adversary queries x*. The adversary sees a random-looking value and cannot distinguish programmed from fresh. This is how RSA-FDH, OAEP, and Schnorr proofs embed their challenges.

questions.question: What does the CGH theorem (Canetti-Goldreich-Halevi) say about ROM proofs?
options: There exist schemes that are ROM-secure but insecure with any concrete hash function
All ROM-secure schemes are also secure in the standard model
Replacing the random oracle with SHA-256 always preserves security
ROM proofs are only valid for symmetric-key schemes
questions.explanation: CGH 1998: there exist contrived (but valid) signature and encryption schemes that are provably secure in the ROM yet insecure when the oracle is replaced by any concrete efficiently-computable hash. ROM proofs are therefore heuristic — not unconditional guarantees.

questions.question: You want a hash function with 128-bit collision security AND 128-bit preimage security. What minimum output length do you need?
options: 256 bits — collision security requires n ≥ 2k, so n ≥ 256 for k=128
128 bits — both attacks require 2^128 work
192 bits — a compromise between preimage and collision security
512 bits — you always need 4k bits to be safe
questions.explanation: Preimage: need n ≥ 128. Collision (birthday): need n ≥ 256. The binding constraint is collision. SHA-256 (n=256) gives exactly 128-bit collision and 256-bit preimage security. SHA-128 would give only 64-bit collision security.

questions.question: A protocol proof says 'the adversary queries the random oracle at most q times'. Why does bounding q matter?
options: All ROM security bounds (preimage q/2^n, collision q²/2^n) degrade with q — more queries = higher advantage
The oracle slows down with more queries, making the adversary computationally weaker
Bounding q is just a formality; real security does not depend on it
Only collision security depends on q; preimage security is unconditional
questions.explanation: ROM advantages are proportional to q: preimage ≤ q/2^n, collision ≤ q²/2^(n+1). Every additional query increases the adversary's chance. Bounding q to polynomial(n) keeps the advantage negligible — this is why the ROM is compatible with the PPT adversary model.

questions.question: In a ROM security proof, how does the reduction handle an adversary's hash query H(m)?
options: It either returns a pre-programmed value (if m was programmed) or lazy-samples a fresh random value and records it
It evaluates SHA-256(m) and returns the result
It rejects the query and forces the adversary to guess
It returns the same value for every query to detect patterns
questions.explanation: The reduction maintains a table. For pre-programmed inputs, it returns the programmed value. For new inputs, it samples a uniform random value, stores it (for consistency), and returns it. From the adversary's view this is identical to a true random function.
